Peu après que la pandémie s’est installé: Soon after the pandemic settled into our lives, the tragedy in the CHSLDs broke out. Shocked, unsettled and saddened, Quebecers looked for answers to events never seen before. How do you explain the incomprehensible?
Il ne suffit que de quelques paroles pou: It takes only a few words for the wisdom of Lucille Nadeau-Brunet, accumulated over her 96 years of life, to fill the small living room of her apartment in northern Montréal.
Choquée par l’hécatombe causée par la pa: Shocked by the carnage the pandemic caused in long-term care centres (CHSLDs), she made it her duty to say out loud what she believes is wrong. In an open letter that went viral after it was published on Facebook, she calls for a “third-age revolution.” Fully independent herself, she laments that “no one asks” older people what kind of lifestyle they want.
« La personne âgée est marginalisée, et: “Older people are marginalized, and they are not included, or very little, in the big decisions that affect the future of society, let alone those that concern them,” explains the woman, in a soprano voice marked by the passage of time. She believes that the dramatic situation brought to light in Quebec’s CHSLDs is only a symptom of this phenomenon, which results in older people being seen as “unnecessary beings.”
Afin de s’assurer de limiter la contagio: To ensure that contagion was limited, the government put in place draconian measures that often left people in precarious situations, deprived of the support provided by their families.
Pour éviter qu’un tel drame se reproduis: To prevent such a tragedy from happening again, Ms. Nadeau-Brunet calls for the creation of an “aging policy”: “It is important that Quebec have one, and that it thereby officially recognize the place and role of seniors, as well as the services that must be provided to them.”
<strong>Des petits soins qui valent beau: Small acts of care that mean a lot
Également âgée de 96 ans, Thérèse Tasche: Also 96 years old, Thérèse Taschereau has lived for almost 10 years with her daughter, José Taschereau, and José’s husband in the suburbs of Québec City. She lives in an extension built onto their house, which lets her keep a certain degree of independence, something that, according to José, would not be possible in a CHSLD. “She makes her breakfast, does a few dishes, picks up the dog hair off the floor,” says José, who is well aware of how much these small tasks matter in helping her mother feel valued in the family nest.
Les témoignages émanant des CHSLD contra: The accounts coming out of the CHSLDs stand in contrast to the reality Thérèse has lived during the pandemic. Although her weekly hair appointment was cancelled for several weeks, the daily life of the woman nicknamed “Gangan” has remained more or less the same. José is aware of how lucky her mother is to live with her: “I don’t think everyone can stay at home until the end. […] It’s not possible for everyone. I’m happy to do it, but the right conditions have to be in place for it to work.”
